claim: Structured Illumination Microscopy (SIM) combined with machine learning algorithms enables high throughput analysis and classification of virus structure.
source: Here, we report on a new methodology which combines Structured Illumination Microscopy (SIM) with machine learning algorithms to image and classify the structure of large populations of biopharmaceutical viruses with high resolution.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this as the main finding of the study.

claim: The method offers information on virus morphology that can be linked with functional performance.
source: The method offers information on virus morphology that can ultimately be linked with functional performance.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of the method in the abstract.

claim: The approach was demonstrated on Newcastle Disease Virus used for oncolytic viriotherapy.
source: We demonstrate the approach on viruses produced for oncolytic viriotherapy (Newcastle Disease Virus) and vaccine development (Influenza).
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the viruses studied.

claim: The approach was demonstrated on Influenza virus used for vaccine development.
source: We demonstrate the approach on viruses produced for oncolytic viriotherapy (Newcastle Disease Virus) and vaccine development (Influenza).
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the viruses studied.

claim: The method enables rapid assessment of viral production quality with high throughput.
source: This unique tool enables the rapid assessment of the quality of viral production with high throughput obviating the need for traditional batch testing methods which are complex and time consuming.
evidence: The abstract states this as a key advantage of the method.

claim: Traditional batch testing methods for virus quality are complex and time consuming.
source: This unique tool enables the rapid assessment of the quality of viral production with high throughput obviating the need for traditional batch testing methods which are complex and time consuming.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The method works on non-purified samples from pooled harvest fluids directly from the production line.
source: We show that our method also works on non-purified samples from pooled harvest fluids directly from the production line.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this capability.

claim: Super-resolution microscopy has potential to unravel details of virus structure and replication.
source: The potential of super-resolution microscopy (SRM) to unravel details of the structure and replication of viruses was recognised early on in the development of the methodology (Betzig et al., 2006; Müller and Heilemann, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SRM has been used to provide unprecedented insights into viral protein architecture.
source: Since then, SRM has been used to provide unprecedented insights into viral protein architecture (Laine et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015; Gray et al., 2016; Albecka et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Previous work on virus structure using SRM focused on techniques that achieve the highest theoretical resolution such as STED and SMLM.
source: Previous work has focused on those SRM techniques that achieve the highest theoretical resolution, such as Stimulated Emission Depletion (STED) (Hell and Wichmann, 1994) and Single Molecule Localisation Microscopy (SMLM) (Rust et al., 2006; Heilemann et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: STED and SMLM offer high fidelity data but require long acquisition times, limiting their application to static samples at low throughput.
source: Whilst offering high fidelity data, the downside is the associated long acquisition time required by these methods, limiting their application to the imaging of static samples at low throughput.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of these techniques.

claim: Structured Illumination Microscopy (SIM) is a much faster technique than STED and SMLM, although inferior in spatial resolution.
source: A much faster technique, although inferior in spatial resolution, is Structured Illumination Microscopy (SIM) (Gustafsson, 2000; Heintzmann and Cremer, 1999) and this has been applied to study large viruses such as the prototypic poxvirus (Gray et al., 2016; Horsington et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: SIM has been applied to study large viruses such as the prototypic poxvirus.
source: A much faster technique, although inferior in spatial resolution, is Structured Illumination Microscopy (SIM) (Gustafsson, 2000; Heintzmann and Cremer, 1999) and this has been applied to study large viruses such as the prototypic poxvirus (Gray et al., 2016; Horsington et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: There is a need to identify and analyse classes of structures within large viral populations in the biotechnology industry.
source: In addition to understanding the structure of viruses, there is also a need to identify and analyse classes of structures within large viral populations, especially in the biotechnology industry where virus quality is often compromised by large scale production operations and the virus product is often characterised by significant morphological heterogeneities.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the work.

claim: Virus quality is often compromised by large scale production operations in the biotechnology industry.
source: In addition to understanding the structure of viruses, there is also a need to identify and analyse classes of structures within large viral populations, especially in the biotechnology industry where virus quality is often compromised by large scale production operations and the virus product is often characterised by significant morphological heterogeneities.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: Virus products are often characterised by significant morphological heterogeneities.
source: In addition to understanding the structure of viruses, there is also a need to identify and analyse classes of structures within large viral populations, especially in the biotechnology industry where virus quality is often compromised by large scale production operations and the virus product is often characterised by significant morphological heterogeneities.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: Campaigns of influenza immunization rely heavily on the timely and efficient production of specific virus strains.
source: In particular, campaigns of influenza immunization rely heavily on the timely and efficient production of specific virus strains.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: A deeper understanding of the structural heterogeneity of oncolytic viruses such as Newcastle Disease Virus would enable optimization of production processes.
source: Similarly, a deeper understanding of the structural heterogeneity of oncolytic viruses such as Newcastle Disease Virus (NDV) (Ganar et al., 2014; Lichty et al., 2014) would enable optimization of the production processes and in turn improve the development of viriotherapy.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation with supporting citations.

claim: Understanding structural heterogeneity of oncolytic viruses would improve the development of viriotherapy.
source: Similarly, a deeper understanding of the structural heterogeneity of oncolytic viruses such as Newcastle Disease Virus (NDV) (Ganar et al., 2014; Lichty et al., 2014) would enable optimization of the production processes and in turn improve the development of viriotherapy.
evidence: This is stated as a potential outcome.

claim: Quantifying and understanding structural heterogeneity and relating it to virus efficacy requires imaging large numbers of viruses at sufficient spatial resolution.
source: However, quantifying and understanding this structural heterogeneity and relating it to virus efficacy requires the imaging of large numbers of viruses at sufficient spatial resolution to reveal characteristic morphological details.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement for the field.

claim: Virus characterization is typically achieved by extracting batches from the production process with elaborate purification and preparation steps before characterisation by Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM).
source: Typically, this is achieved by extracting batches from the production process, with elaborate subsequent purification and preparation steps before characterisation by Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) (Gad, 2007; Goldsmith and Miller, 2009; Brenner and Horne, 1959).
evidence: This is stated as current practice with supporting citations.

claim: TEM can achieve relatively high imaging throughput if the highest resolution is not necessary.
source: Although TEM can achieve relatively high imaging throughput if the highest resolution is not necessary, its contrast remains unspecific and therefore does not typically permit discerning the presence of particular proteins in the virus envelope.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of TEM.

claim: TEM contrast remains unspecific and does not typically permit discerning the presence of particular proteins in the virus envelope.
source: Although TEM can achieve relatively high imaging throughput if the highest resolution is not necessary, its contrast remains unspecific and therefore does not typically permit discerning the presence of particular proteins in the virus envelope.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of TEM.

claim: The typical signal-to-noise ratios achieved by TEM are not sufficient to permit automated, robust and efficient downstream analysis of structural features at the single particle level.
source: Also, the typical signal-to-noise ratios achieved by TEM are not sufficient to permit automated, robust and efficient downstream analysis of structural features at the single particle level.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of TEM.

claim: It is challenging for TEM to be of practical use during production operations.
source: It is therefore challenging for TEM to be of practical use during production operations.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on TEM limitations.

claim: Rapid high resolution imaging with TIRF-SIM combined with machine learning offers a great opportunity to circumvent problems with traditional virus characterization methods.
source: Here, we demonstrate that rapid high resolution imaging with Total Internal Reflection SIM fluorescence microscopy (TIRF-SIM) (Shao et al., 2011; Kner et al., 2009; Young et al., 2016), combined with a machine learning (ML) approach to analyse and classify structures in virus batches offer a great opportunity to circumvent these problems.
evidence: This is stated as the main contribution with supporting citations.

claim: MiLeSIM is an efficient combination of SRM, ML-based classification and advanced image analysis for quantification of morphological heterogeneities in large virus populations.
source: We present MiLeSIM (Machine Learning Structured Illumination Microscopy) as an efficient combination of SRM, ML-based classification (Van Valen et al., 2016; Sommer et al., 2011) and advanced image analysis for the quantification of morphological heterogeneities in large virus populations.
evidence: This is the definition of the method with supporting citations.

claim: ML algorithms are used to perform classification of super-resolved images of heterogeneous virus populations into particle classes with distinct structural features.
source: We use ML algorithms to perform a classification of super-resolved images of a heterogeneous virus population into particle classes with distinct and characteristic structural features (e.g. spherical, filamentous).
evidence: This describes the methodology used.

claim: Classified subpopulations are further analysed through image analysis pipelines specifically adapted for each structural class.
source: The classified subpopulations are then further analysed through image analysis pipelines that are specifically adapted for each structural class.
evidence: This describes the methodology used.

claim: Appropriate model fitting can lead to precision in structural parameters beyond the resolution of the images used.
source: We and others have shown that appropriate model fitting can lead to precision in structural parameters beyond the resolution of the images used (Laine et al., 2015; Manetsberger et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The method combines speed and specificity and allows an in-depth exploration of large virus populations that is unachievable by TEM.
source: The method combines speed and specificity and allows an in-depth exploration of large virus populations that is unachievable by TEM.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the method.

claim: The method has potentials in the industrial production of viruses for oncolytic viriotherapy and vaccine development.
source: The method has potentials in the industrial production of viruses, for example for oncolytic viriotherapy and vaccine development.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application.

claim: TIRF-SIM is the method of choice to investigate virus structure at high-throughput with a spatial resolution reaching ~90 nm.
source: First, we compare TIRF-SIM with alternative imaging modalities and show that it is the method of choice to investigate virus structure at high-throughput (~220 virus particles/s, see Supplementary Note 1) with a spatial resolution reaching ~90 nm.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the comparison study.

claim: TIRF-SIM can image approximately 220 virus particles per second.
source: First, we compare TIRF-SIM with alternative imaging modalities and show that it is the method of choice to investigate virus structure at high-throughput (~220 virus particles/s, see Supplementary Note 1) with a spatial resolution reaching ~90 nm.
evidence: This is stated as a measured throughput.

claim: Large datasets obtained with TIRF-SIM are fed into an ML algorithm for automated classification of Newcastle Disease Virus and live attenuated influenza virus vaccines.
source: The large datasets obtained with TIRF-SIM are then fed into an ML algorithm for the automated classification of Newcastle Disease Virus (NDV) and live attenuated influenza virus (LAIV) vaccines, enabling further shape-specific quantitative analyses for a structural description of viral subpopulations.
evidence: This describes the methodology applied.

claim: The MiLeSIM approach is a powerful analysis tool for biotechnological processes involving virus production in industry and research laboratories.
source: The purpose of our study is to validate the MiLeSIM approach as a powerful analysis tool for biotechnological processes involving virus production both in industry and in the research laboratory.
evidence: This is stated as the purpose of the study.

claim: Three common SRM modalities were explored and compared for structural investigation of purified NDV virus: dSTORM, STED and TIRF-SIM.
source: First, we explored and compared three common SRM modalities for the structural investigation of purified NDV virus, namely direct stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy, dSTORM, stimulated emission depletion microscopy, STED and TIRF-SIM.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach.

claim: NDV viruses were labelled for the envelope glycoprotein Hemagglutinin-Neuraminidase (HN).
source: NDV viruses were labelled for the envelope glycoprotein Hemagglutinin-Neuraminidase (HN) and imaged with all three SRM imaging techniques (see Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the sample preparation.

claim: Labelling for HN allows direct and specific observation of the shape of virus particles.
source: Labelling for HN allows us to directly and specifically observe the shape of the virus particles.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the labeling strategy.

claim: TIRF-SIM provides clear structural details to discern filamentous, spherical and rod-like structures in large NDV populations.
source: TIRF-SIM provides clear structural details to discern filamentous, spherical and rod-like structures in large NDV populations.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the imaging.

claim: Improving resolution beyond the ~90 nm offered by TIRF-SIM comes at a significant cost in acquisition times and throughput.
source: It is clear that improving resolution beyond the ~90 nm offered by TIRF-SIM (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1(b)) comes at a significant cost in acquisition times and throughput.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the comparison, with reference to figure data.

claim: Although dSTORM and STED offer theoretically higher resolution than SIM, the images obtained with these methods do not reveal additional structural details that are not also resolved by TIRF-SIM images.
source: Furthermore, although dSTORM and STED offer theoretically higher resolution than SIM, the images obtained with these methods do not reveal additional structural details that are not also resolved by TIRF-SIM images.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the comparison.

claim: The ~2 fold resolution improvement provided by TIRF-SIM is sufficient for the structural study presented.
source: This indicates that the ~2 fold resolution improvement provided by TIRF-SIM is sufficient for the structural study presented here.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the comparison.

claim: EM has traditionally been the method of choice for observing sub-diffraction structures of virus particles.
source: Traditionally, EM has been the method of choice for observing sub-diffraction structures of virus particles (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2 for examples of particles).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with reference to figure.

claim: TIRF-SIM can offer significant advantages compared to EM.
source: Here we show that TIRF-SIM can offer significant advantages compared to EM (summarized in Table 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to table.

claim: The improvement in molecular specificity of TIRF-SIM allows an unambiguous identification of viral components.
source: The improvement in molecular specificity allows an unambiguous identification of viral components; the high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) furthermore enables a robust and straightforward application of further image analysis steps (identification and classification of virus particles).
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of TIRF-SIM.

claim: The high signal-to-noise ratio of TIRF-SIM enables robust and straightforward application of further image analysis steps.
source: The improvement in molecular specificity allows an unambiguous identification of viral components; the high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) furthermore enables a robust and straightforward application of further image analysis steps (identification and classification of virus particles).
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of TIRF-SIM.

claim: The capability of investigating unpurified and aqueous samples makes TIRF-SIM ideally suited to the present application.
source: Also, the capability of investigating unpurified and aqueous samples makes TIRF-SIM ideally suited to the present application.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of TIRF-SIM.

claim: TIRF-SIM images show a number of stereotypical virus structures in NDV samples labelled for HN, indicating large morphological diversity in virus populations.
source: The images obtained with TIRF-SIM show a number of stereotypical virus structures in NDV samples labelled for HN, indicating a large morphological diversity in the virus populations that may stem from variability occurring during viral replication or at the purification stage.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the imaging.

claim: Morphological diversity in virus populations may stem from variability occurring during viral replication or at the purification stage.
source: The images obtained with TIRF-SIM show a number of stereotypical virus structures in NDV samples labelled for HN, indicating a large morphological diversity in the virus populations that may stem from variability occurring during viral replication or at the purification stage.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation.

claim: Understanding the origins and consequences of virus heterogeneity informs on the life cycle of the virus and can provide essential insights into the virus production process.
source: Understanding the origins and consequences of such heterogeneity informs not only on the life cycle of the virus but can also provide essential insights into the virus production process to manufacturers of virus-based therapeutics.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the work.

claim: An automated classification of virus shapes would enable the quantification of virus heterogeneity and permit further analysis of each individual class independently.
source: An automated classification of virus shapes would enable the quantification of virus heterogeneity and permit further analysis of each individual class independently.
evidence: This is stated as a goal of the method.

claim: Individual virus particles are first identified by automated segmentation and then fed to the ML routine for classification.
source: Individual virus particles are first identified by automated segmentation and then fed to the ML routine for classification.
evidence: This describes the workflow.

claim: A supervised ML algorithm (random forest algorithm) was used to ensure robustness and ease of implementation.
source: We used a supervised ML algorithm (here a random forest algorithm (Breiman, 2001)) to ensure the robustness of the method and for ease of implementation.
evidence: This describes the choice of algorithm with citation.

claim: Six major structural classes were identified in NDV samples: long and short filamentous, small and large spherical, rod-like and unknown structures.
source: We identified six major structural classes in the NDV samples which we divide into long and short filamentous, small and large spherical, rod-like and unknown structures.
evidence: This describes the classification scheme.

claim: The unknown class is made of clumps of viral material with no consistent and identifiable shapes.
source: The unknown class is made of clumps of viral material with no consistent and identifiable shapes.
evidence: This defines the unknown class.

claim: Non-specific bindings of antibodies appear as rare, dim and small point-like structures that could easily be discriminated and excluded from further analysis.
source: A control sample that was prepared identically to the other samples except without virus particles present allowed us to identify that non-specific bindings of antibodies appear as rare, dim and small point-like structures that could easily be discriminated and excluded from further analysis.
evidence: This describes findings from the control experiment.

claim: The filamentous class is further analysed by automatic extraction of the linear backbone of structures and measurement of their length.
source: The filamentous (long and short) class is further analysed by automatic extraction of the linear backbone of structures and measurement of their length.
evidence: This describes the analysis method for filamentous structures.

claim: The width of filamentous structures appeared to be limited by the resolution of the imaging technique (~90 nm for TIRF-SIM).
source: The width of these filamentous structures appeared to be limited by the resolution of the imaging technique (~90 nm for TIRF-SIM, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1, but also observed in higher resolution approaches such as dSTORM) and therefore, we considered the filamentous class as 1D structures.
evidence: This is stated as an observation with reference to figure.

claim: Filamentous structures were considered as 1D structures because their width is limited by imaging resolution.
source: The width of these filamentous structures appeared to be limited by the resolution of the imaging technique (~90 nm for TIRF-SIM, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1, but also observed in higher resolution approaches such as dSTORM) and therefore, we considered the filamentous class as 1D structures.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological decision based on observations.

claim: Spherical structures were analysed by estimating their equivalent radius from the area of the particle.
source: The spherical structures were analysed by estimating their equivalent radius from the area of the particle.
evidence: This describes the analysis method for spherical structures.

claim: A model-based fitting approach was used to fit rod-like viral particles and obtain length and width parameters.
source: A similar model-based fitting approach was used to fit rod-like viral particles and to obtain length and width parameters for this structural class (see Materials and methods section and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for details).
evidence: This describes the analysis method for rod-like structures with reference to methods and figure.

claim: The structural classification was performed using a supervised ML algorithm which allows for rapid and automated classification of large datasets.
source: The structural classification was performed using a supervised ML algorithm which allows for rapid and automated classification of large datasets.
evidence: This describes the classification approach.

claim: The choice of algorithm and set of features were optimised to maximise the overall accuracy of the model based on the training dataset comprising 370 manually annotated particles.
source: The choice of algorithm and the set of features (often called predictors) extracted for each identified particle were optimised to maximise the overall accuracy of the model based on the training dataset (comprising of 370 manually annotated particles).
evidence: This describes the optimization approach.

claim: Model accuracy is defined as the fraction of correctly classified particles across all classes.
source: Here, the model accuracy is defined as the fraction of correctly classified particles across all classes.
evidence: This defines the accuracy metric.

claim: Predictors were selected based on basic structural features, Hu's image moments, features from AlexNet CNN, and SURF features.
source: Figure 3(a) describes the list of chosen individual features (selected from basic shapes features, Hu's image moments (Hu, 1962), features obtained from the pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) AlexNet (Krizhevsky et al., 2012) and from Speeded Up Robust Features, SURF (Bay et al., 2008)).
evidence: This describes the feature selection with citations and reference to figure.

claim: Basic structural features and Hu's moments were chosen because they are rotationally and translationally invariant.
source: The predictors were selected based on the following criteria: basic structural features of the particles (e.g. area, eccentricity) and Hu's moments were chosen because they are rotationally and translationally invariant.
evidence: This explains the rationale for feature selection.

claim: A feature selection approach was designed for AlexNet and SURF features based on maximising the standard deviation across different structural classes.
source: For the features from AlexNet and SURF a feature selection approach was designed based on maximising the standard deviation across the different structural classes.
evidence: This describes the feature selection method.

claim: The feature selection approach constitutes a more rational choice compared to simple principal component analysis (PCA), which does not typically take class information into account.
source: This approach constitutes a more rational choice compared to simple principal component analysis (PCA), which does not typically take the information regarding the classes into account, therefore our method selects for predictors that have high potential for class discrimination.
evidence: This explains the advantage of the chosen approach.

claim: Data reduction narrowed down the number of predictors to six for AlexNet and six for SURF.
source: This data reduction narrowed down the number of predictors to six for AlexNet and six for SURF.
evidence: This describes the outcome of feature selection.

claim: A total of 24 predictors was chosen: seven based on basic shapes, 5 of Hu's image moments, six from AlexNet and six from SURF.
source: A total of 24 predictors was finally chosen: seven based on basic shapes (area, ratio of axis lengths, eccentricity, solidity, perimeter-to-area, mean intensity, standard deviation of pixel intensities), 5 of Hu's image moments (Hu1, Hu4, Hu5, Hu6 and Phi4), six features obtained from the pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) AlexNet and six from a SURF bag of features.
evidence: This lists the final set of predictors.

claim: Some predictors support classification across specific classes better than other combinations.
source: Panels described in Figure 3(b) show examples of scatter plot from arbitrarily chosen pairs of predictors highlighting that some predictors support classification across specific classes better than other combinations (identifiable clusters of certain classes).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the scatter plots with reference to figure.

claim: The confusion matrix highlights effective true positive rate (TPR) and positive predictive values (PPV) across different classes with a model accuracy of 88.4%.
source: The confusion matrix (Figure 3(c)) highlights the effective true positive rate (TPR) and positive predictive values (PPV) across the different classes with a model accuracy of 88.4%.
evidence: This reports the classification performance with reference to figure.

claim: Some long filamentous viruses are misclassified as small filamentous.
source: We note that some long filamentous viruses are misclassified as small filamentous, some small filamentous are misclassified as small spherical and that, on occasion, some unknown structures populate the predicted long and large spherical structure classes.
evidence: This describes observed misclassifications.

claim: Some small filamentous viruses are misclassified as small spherical.
source: We note that some long filamentous viruses are misclassified as small filamentous, some small filamentous are misclassified as small spherical and that, on occasion, some unknown structures populate the predicted long and large spherical structure classes.
evidence: This describes observed misclassifications.

claim: Some unknown structures populate the predicted long and large spherical structure classes.
source: We note that some long filamentous viruses are misclassified as small filamentous, some small filamentous are misclassified as small spherical and that, on occasion, some unknown structures populate the predicted long and large spherical structure classes.
evidence: This describes observed misclassifications.

claim: Considering the simple shapes of these viruses, it is expected that a small fraction of particles are misclassified as structures with close resemblance.
source: Considering the simple shapes of these viruses, it is expected that a small fraction of particles are misclassified as structures with close resemblance.
evidence: This is stated as an expected outcome.

claim: The scoring of predictors indicates the average accuracy of each individual predictor.
source: The scoring of the predictors presented in Figure 3(d) indicates the average accuracy of each individual predictor.
evidence: This describes the predictor scoring with reference to figure.

claim: A high score indicates a high capacity to discriminate between different classes.
source: A high score indicates a high capacity to discriminate between different classes.
evidence: This explains the interpretation of the scoring.

claim: The scoring was performed by measuring the accuracy of the classification for many combinations of predictors and distributing the accuracy score across the predictors tested.
source: The scoring was performed by measuring the accuracy of the classification for many combinations of predictors and distributing the accuracy score across the predictors tested (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This describes the scoring methodology.

claim: The scoring method was repeated across more than 13,000 different combinations of predictors.
source: This method was repeated and scores represent averages across >13,000 different combinations of predictors.
evidence: This describes the extent of the scoring analysis.

claim: A total of approximately 6500 particles were analysed using MiLeSIM.
source: We analysed a total of ~6500 particles using MiLeSIM and established that 49.7% of NDV particles presented a filamentous shape whereas the large spherical, small spherical and rods represent 18.6%, 7.8% and 7.3% of the total population, respectively (Figure 4(a)).
evidence: This reports the sample size with reference to figure.

claim: 49.7% of NDV particles presented a filamentous shape.
source: We analysed a total of ~6500 particles using MiLeSIM and established that 49.7% of NDV particles presented a filamentous shape whereas the large spherical, small spherical and rods represent 18.6%, 7.8% and 7.3% of the total population, respectively (Figure 4(a)).
evidence: This reports the classification results with reference to figure.

claim: Large spherical NDV particles represent 18.6% of the total population.
source: We analysed a total of ~6500 particles using MiLeSIM and established that 49.7% of NDV particles presented a filamentous shape whereas the large spherical, small spherical and rods represent 18.6%, 7.8% and 7.3% of the total population, respectively (Figure 4(a)).
evidence: This reports the classification results with reference to figure.

claim: Small spherical NDV particles represent 7.8% of the total population.
source: We analysed a total of ~6500 particles using MiLeSIM and established that 49.7% of NDV particles presented a filamentous shape whereas the large spherical, small spherical and rods represent 18.6%, 7.8% and 7.3% of the total population, respectively (Figure 4(a)).
evidence: This reports the classification results with reference to figure.

claim: Rod-shaped NDV particles represent 7.3% of the total population.
source: We analysed a total of ~6500 particles using MiLeSIM and established that 49.7% of NDV particles presented a filamentous shape whereas the large spherical, small spherical and rods represent 18.6%, 7.8% and 7.3% of the total population, respectively (Figure 4(a)).
evidence: This reports the classification results with reference to figure.

claim: Both long filamentous and large spherical NDV particles are well described by a Gamma distribution.
source: We observe that both long filamentous and large spherical are well described by a Gamma distribution whereas the small filamentous and small spherical are well described by a Gaussian distribution.
evidence: This reports the statistical distribution fitting results.

claim: Small filamentous and small spherical NDV particles are well described by a Gaussian distribution.
source: We observe that both long filamentous and large spherical are well described by a Gamma distribution whereas the small filamentous and small spherical are well described by a Gaussian distribution.
evidence: This reports the statistical distribution fitting results.

claim: The model-fitting applied to rod-shaped particles allows extraction of both width and length of each particle.
source: The model-fitting applied to the rod-shaped particles (see Materials and methods and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for details) allows the extraction of both the width and length of each particle.
evidence: This describes the capability of the model-fitting approach with reference to methods and figure.

claim: For NDV, the mean length of long filamentous particles is 650 ± 430 nm.
source: We estimated the mean and standard deviation of the structural parameters from the distributions and obtained: LLF = 650 ± 430 nm, LSF = 200 ± 100 nm, DLS = 338 ± 94 nm, DSS = 190 ± 10 nm.
evidence: This reports the measured structural parameters.

claim: For NDV, the mean length of short filamentous particles is 200 ± 100 nm.
source: We estimated the mean and standard deviation of the structural parameters from the distributions and obtained: LLF = 650 ± 430 nm, LSF = 200 ± 100 nm, DLS = 338 ± 94 nm, DSS = 190 ± 10 nm.
evidence: This reports the measured structural parameters.

claim: For NDV, the mean diameter of large spherical particles is 338 ± 94 nm.
source: We estimated the mean and standard deviation of the structural parameters from the distributions and obtained: LLF = 650 ± 430 nm, LSF = 200 ± 100 nm, DLS = 338 ± 94 nm, DSS = 190 ± 10 nm.
evidence: This reports the measured structural parameters.

claim: For NDV, the mean diameter of small spherical particles is 190 ± 10 nm.
source: We estimated the mean and standard deviation of the structural parameters from the distributions and obtained: LLF = 650 ± 430 nm, LSF = 200 ± 100 nm, DLS = 338 ± 94 nm, DSS = 190 ± 10 nm.
evidence: This reports the measured structural parameters.

claim: For NDV rod-shaped particles, the mean width is 135 ± 30 nm.
source: For the rod-shaped particles, we observed that the width WRD = 135 ± 30 nm and the length LRD = 610 ± 350 nm (all rounded to two significant figures, ± represents the standard deviation of the distribution).
evidence: This reports the measured structural parameters.

claim: For NDV rod-shaped particles, the mean length is 610 ± 350 nm.
source: For the rod-shaped particles, we observed that the width WRD = 135 ± 30 nm and the length LRD = 610 ± 350 nm (all rounded to two significant figures, ± represents the standard deviation of the distribution).
evidence: This reports the measured structural parameters.

claim: Rod-shaped particle dimensions are distributed around two populations.
source: These values are distributed around two populations as shown on the contour plot in Figure 4(d).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with reference to figure.

claim: The radius analysis based on the area of the particle constitutes an overestimate of the physical radius due to broadening caused by the point-spread function.
source: However, we note that the radius analysis based on the area of the particle used here constitutes an overestimate of the physical radius of the particle due to the broadening caused by the point-spread function.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the area-based method.

claim: It is possible to estimate a more accurate diameter of spherical structures by using the ELM analysis.
source: It is possible to estimate a more accurate diameter of the underlying spherical structures by using the ELM analysis.
evidence: This is stated as an alternative method.

claim: The ELM diameter obtained for large spherical NDV particles is 220 ± 69 nm.
source: The results obtained from the ELM analysis of the large spherical structures are shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1(a). The ELM diameter obtained for the large spherical particles (220 ± 69 nm) is in good agreement with an area-based diameter of 338 nm and a resolution of 90 nm.
evidence: This reports the ELM analysis results with reference to figure.
